Zebah
zē'bä
n. (one of the two kings of Midian pursued and slain by Gideon; his name means sacrifice)
From Hebrew Zebach, a sacrifice or slaughtered victim — a name whose sense was answered in the manner of his death. Scripture almost always pairs him with Zalmunna.

Biblical Definition

Zebah is named eleven times in Judges and never once alone. He and Zalmunna are the two surviving kings of Midian after the rout of the three hundred, and Gideon's pursuit of them across the Jordan is one of the grimmest passages in the book. Faint and still chasing, he asked bread of the men of Succoth and was mocked: are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men (Jdg 8:15)? He took the kings anyway — “when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian” (Jdg 8:12) — came back and taught the men of Succoth with thorns and briers. Then came the question that explains the whole chase: “What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king” (Jdg 8:18). They had killed Gideon's brothers. This was blood vengeance as well as holy war. He ordered his firstborn son to kill them; the boy was afraid; and the kings themselves asked for a soldier's death: “Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna” (Jdg 8:21). Asaph keeps them as a byword: make all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna (Psa 83:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Zebah; in sacred history he is one of the two kings of Midian taken and slain by Gideon beyond Jordan.

expand to see more

ZEBAH, n. One of the two kings of Midian in the days of Gideon.

He is always named with Zalmunna, his fellow king.

They fled beyond Jordan with fifteen thousand men, and were pursued and taken at Karkor.

They had slain the brethren of Gideon at Tabor, and he required their blood.

The psalmist makes them a byword for the princes of the enemies of God's people.

Key Scripture

Jdg 8:5 — "And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian."

Jdg 8:12 — "And when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and discomfited all the host."

Jdg 8:18 — "Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king."

Jdg 8:21 — "Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks."

Modern Corruption

Gideon is flattened into a straightforward hero, when Judges deliberately shows the same man growing harsher through the chapter and ending in an ephod that became a snare to all Israel.

expand to see more

The children's-story Gideon — fleece, trumpets, three hundred men — stops before Judges 8, and Judges 8 is where the author is going. The man who began by asking for signs ends by threshing the elders of his own countrymen with thorns, tearing down a tower and killing its people, executing kings for family blood, and taking the golden earrings of the spoil to make an ephod “which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house” (Jdg 8:27). The book is not endorsing this trajectory; it is recording it, in a volume whose refrain is that every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Scripture's heroes are given to us with their sins attached, which is one of the strongest evidences that it is not propaganda.

The second thing to name is the modern discomfort with blood vengeance, which usually produces either a squeamish silence or an attack on the text. Judges reports a world in which the avenger of blood was a recognized office, later regulated by the law of Moses with cities of refuge to restrain it. Scripture's trajectory is toward the removal of private vengeance altogether: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). Justice is not abolished; it is transferred to the magistrate and finally to God, who will not let one drop of innocent blood go unanswered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Zebach (H2078), Zebah, sacrifice; zabach (H2076), to slaughter, sacrifice; radaph (H7291), to pursue; go'el haddam, avenger of blood; Midyan (H4080), Midian.

expand to see more

Hebrew Zebach (H2078) — Zebah; the name is the ordinary word for a sacrifice.

Hebrew zabach (H2076) — to slaughter, to sacrifice; the root of the name.

Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, chase; the verb governing the whole of Jdg 8.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-avenger; the office Gideon exercised at Tabor.

Hebrew Midyan (H4080) — Midian; their nation, broken by three hundred men.

Usage

"“I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna” — faint, and still chasing."

"“Each one resembled the children of a king” — the answer that named the debt."

"“All their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” — a psalm keeps them as a byword."
